titulo.texto: Donkey Jawbone and Mask for the Dance of the Diablos

frase_gancho.texto: A mask with horns and a mane, made for a dance that speaks of Africa.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the mask of the coast, we move on to painting. Look for a mural of people from the different regions of Oaxaca, painted in their clothing, with their festivals and their trade.

guion_corto.texto: This mask and the donkey jawbone that goes with it belong to the Dance of the Diablos, which is performed in the Afro-Mexican communities of the Costa Chica of Oaxaca and Guerrero. The mask has real animal horns, horsehair manes and long beards, and it inspires fear and laughter at the same time. The donkey jawbone is an instrument: it is scraped or struck to produce a rough, rhythmic sound. The dancers move through the streets stomping their feet, to the sound of a violin and instruments made from everyday objects. The dance is performed above all at the festivals of All Saints and the Day of the Dead. It is a tradition that speaks of Mexico’s African heritage, the so-called third root.

guion_largo.texto:
Among the masks you have seen, this one is the noisiest. Animal horns, horsehair manes, black beards. And beside it, an unexpected instrument: the jawbone of a donkey. It is scraped with a stick or struck, and the loose teeth rattle like a ratchet. This is the Dance of the Diablos, and it comes from a part of Mexico that is often forgotten: the Costa Chica of Oaxaca and Guerrero, with its Afro-Mexican communities.

To understand it, we have to look back. During the colonial period, thousands of Africans arrived in New Spain, most of them enslaved. Many ended up on the haciendas and along the coasts. Over time, their descendants formed communities of their own in places like the Costa Chica, where they preserved music, food, words and festivals. They are sometimes called “the third root” of Mexico, alongside the Indigenous and the Spanish.

The dance is performed above all at All Saints and on the Day of the Dead. The dancers, dressed as devils, go through the town, dance in homes and in the streets, and receive food, drink and tips. They are accompanied by a violin and several instruments made from everyday objects, among them the jawbone, the scraped tin can and the charrasca. It is a noisy, mocking festival, full of energy.

Why devils? There are several interpretations. One says that enslaved Africans used the figure of the devil to mock the Spanish overseers and the religion that was imposed on them, without it being easy to punish them, because “they were just celebrating.” Another says that the dance remembers African ancestors and spirits mixed with Catholic ideas. It probably has a bit of both. What matters is that it has been preserved for centuries.

The mask has real horns, manes and beards, and it is made with materials close at hand: leather, wood, sometimes cardboard. Its look is half terrifying, half comic, which is the tone of the whole dance. Like the Viejito of Michoacán and the Cora Judas, whoever puts it on becomes someone else, and for a few hours can say, do and dance what they would not dare to do without it.

There is also a recent history. For a long time, Afro-Mexican communities were barely visible in official history. In the year two thousand nineteen, the Constitution finally recognized Afro-Mexican peoples and communities. The census of two thousand twenty counted more than two and a half million people who identify as Afro-Mexican. That means the voices of these communities are increasingly present.

One curious fact for the road: Vicente Guerrero, one of the heroes of Independence and the second president of the country, had African ancestry and was born in what is today the state of Guerrero. Further on, in the Huastecs and Totonacs Hall, you will see another mask, [that of the Negritos](mna_s18_mascara_negritos), which arose in another region of the country out of other encounters between peoples. Masks, once again, tell us who arrived, who stayed and how they mixed.

texto.Region: Costa Chica of Oaxaca (Collantes, Santiago Llano Grande, Chacahua)
texto.Technique/Material: Carved wood, horsehair, natural horns, cardboard and percussion bone
texto.Function: Ritual paraphernalia of the Dance of the Diablos for All Saints' Day and an affirmation of identity

texto.pregunta: Myth: There were never, and are not now, people of African origin in Mexico.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There have been Afro-Mexican communities since colonial times, above all in the Costa Chica of Oaxaca and Guerrero. They are the third root of the country, and the Constitution has recognized them since two thousand nineteen.
